native_mcp_support.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 and now explicitly documented rather than merely absent. DeepSeek's Responses API compatibility table lists the `mcp` built-in tool (with file_search / code_interpreter / computer_use) as "Ignored"; the Anthropic-compatible endpoint (https://api.deepseek.com/anthropic) lists the `mcp_servers` parameter as "Ignored" and the `mcp_tool_use` / `mcp_tool_result` content blocks as "Not Supported". MCP therefore reaches DeepSeek only when a host/adapter converts MCP tools into OpenAI-style `function` definitions (the same path used when self-hosting behind vLLM/SGLang).

skills_concept.notes: Still no first-party 'skills' or assistant-extension mechanism as of 2026-08-19 (the API docs expose chat completions, the Responses API, thinking mode, tool calls, KV cache, JSON output and FIM only). The closest analogs remain disk-based context caching (KV cache), which cheapens repeated static prefixes such as tool definitions and system prompts, and the `reasoning_effort` budget. No persistent memory, no packaged capability bundles.

release_date.notes: General availability across the DeepSeek app, web ("Expert Mode") and API on 2026-08-13, superseding the 2026-04-24 preview checkpoint. The hosted model id stayed `deepseek-v4-pro`.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Not disclosed on the model card, in the GA announcement or in the API docs. Searched the HF card, api-docs changelog and the GA news post; no training cutoff is published.

context_window_tokens.notes: config.json: max_position_embeddings=1048576 (1M), reached with YaRN RoPE scaling (type=yarn, factor=16, original_max_position_embeddings=65536). The hosted Models & Pricing page independently lists CONTEXT LENGTH 1M for this model.

input_output_shared.notes: One shared 1M pool: context length 1M with MAXIMUM 384K output. Input plus output (including thinking tokens) together consume the window.

max_input_tokens.notes: Derived: context window 1048576 minus the 384K (393216) maximum output = 655360. DeepSeek publishes no separate max-input figure; in practice you can prompt closer to 1M if you reserve less output. (Corrects the previous entry, which stated 671744 while its own note derived 655360.)

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No default published. The Chat Completions reference says only that input plus generated tokens are bounded by the model's context length and defers the range/default to other docs; the Models & Pricing page publishes only the MAXIMUM (384K).

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Models & Pricing states MAXIMUM: 384K output (384*1024 = 393216), covering thinking and final-answer tokens together. The model card recommends a maximum output length of 384K for the `high` and `max` reasoning-effort levels.

extended_context.notes: 1M is the GA window; no separate beta or extended-context tier is offered, so there is nothing above it to record.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Thinking mode emits `reasoning_content`, which is generated output and shares the 384K output ceiling. `reasoning_effort` takes low / high / max (default high; medium and xhigh are mapped to high). Agentic cost trap: for requests carrying `tools`, reasoning_content must be echoed back on every subsequent request or the API returns 400 — so it is billed as output once and then as input on each following step.

tokenizer_family.notes: config.json: vocab_size=129280 — unchanged across V3/V3.2/V4, so token counts are comparable across DeepSeek generations. The 0813 GA checkpoint keeps the V4 tokenizer unchanged from the preview.

tokenizer_access.value: HF AutoTokenizer + the repo's encoding_dsv4 encoding scripts
tokenizer_access.notes: MIT-licensed weights ship the tokenizer. DeepSeek also publishes an offline tokenizer zip at https://cdn.deepseek.com/api-docs/deepseek_v3_tokenizer.zip, but note it is the V3-era package — for exact V4 counts prefer the model repo's own encoding scripts.

count_tokens_method.value: transformers.AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(<repo>).encode(text); or the repo's encoding scripts; or read usage.prompt_tokens from an API response
count_tokens_method.notes: DeepSeek exposes no count-tokens endpoint; the authoritative count is the `usage` object returned with a completion, or a local run of the model's own tokenizer.

image_token_rule.notes: Text-only model; no image modality documented.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Official rule of thumb re-verified 2026-08-19: 1 English character ~ 0.3 token (= ~3.3 chars/token); 1 Chinese character ~ 0.6 token (~1.7 chars/token). Rough estimate only — JSON tool definitions tokenize denser than prose.

function_calling.notes: OpenAI-compatible function calling on /chat/completions, plus function tools on the native Responses API and Anthropic-format tool blocks on the /anthropic endpoint. Tool use works in both thinking and non-thinking modes.

native_mcp.notes: Not MCP-native. The Responses API compatibility table marks the `mcp` built-in tool "Ignored"; the Anthropic-compatible endpoint marks `mcp_servers` "Ignored" and `mcp_tool_use`/`mcp_tool_result` "Not Supported". An MCP host must flatten MCP tools into `function` definitions before sending them.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Upgraded to explicit documentation: on the Responses API "parallel tool calling is always enabled" and `max_tool_calls` is ignored; on the Anthropic-compatible endpoint `disable_parallel_tool_use` is ignored. The model can emit several tool_calls in one assistant turn.

max_tools_hard.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. The cited Chat Completions reference enumerates only hosted aliases for its `model` parameter -- verbatim "Possible values: [`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`]" -- and `deepseek-v4-pro` currently resolves to deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, so the cap does bind anyone calling the hosted endpoint for this checkpoint, and does NOT bind a self-hosted deployment of these weights, where the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang `--tool-call-parser`, `--max-model-len`, KV cache) and the context window consumed by serialized tool definitions set the limits, and an OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of the weights imposes whatever it validates. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the reference states "A max of 128 functions are supported." SCOPE: AGGREGATE -- it counts every function in the request's `tools` array, i.e. all connected MCP servers plus any built-in/host tools combined, not per MCP server. For self-hosted DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 the binding limits are instead the operator's served context length divided by average tool-definition tokens, the empirical selection cliff (see max_tools_practical) and whatever aggregate cap the MCP host imposes (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

max_tools_practical.notes: EMPIRICAL, NOT SPEC, and FAMILY-LEVEL, NOT PER-CHECKPOINT (attribution restated 2026-08-19; tier 4, low confidence). What the cited source actually contains: a single undifferentiated leaderboard entry labelled "DeepSeek V4" reporting 89% single-tool accuracy, 81% at 5 tools and 57% at 20+ tools, with the advice to cap practical tool counts at 15-20 and route/tier above that. It does NOT separate DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek-V4-Flash, does not name a checkpoint (-0813 / -0731), and does not state the serving stack, context length or harness used. The same family-level number is therefore recorded identically on both live checkpoints rather than being split into invented per-variant figures (the same correction convention applied to Gemma's variants and Phi's variants in this dataset). Pro is the flagship of the pair, so a family figure that blends Pro and Flash is if anything pessimistic here; it is still not a measurement of this checkpoint. Scope: AGGREGATE across all connected MCP servers plus built-in tools. Sits far below the hosted API's 128-function cap, and for a self-hosted deployment it is the accuracy cliff -- not any vendor rule -- that binds first.

tool_definition_shape.notes: {type: 'function', function: {name, description, parameters}} on /chat/completions and on the Responses API. The /anthropic endpoint additionally accepts Anthropic tool blocks (name / description / input_schema fully supported). Shape matters for footprint: the same MCP tool serializes to different token counts in the two shapes.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: The serialized `tools` array is part of the prompt and lands in `prompt_tokens`; DeepSeek reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` against that same prompt, so a stable tool-definition prefix is the prime KV-cache candidate. DeepSeek does not state this in one sentence — it follows from the OpenAI-compatible usage object plus the cache guide.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No progressive/deferred tool loading and no server-side tool search. The Responses API supports only function tools, a server-side `web_search`, and the Codex `apply_patch` custom tool; every other built-in (including `mcp`) is ignored. All tool definitions must be resent each request.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Strict mode is a beta feature: call base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/beta", set "strict": true on EVERY function, and set "additionalProperties": false on every object. Supported strict-mode JSON Schema types: object, string, number, integer, boolean, array, enum, anyOf. Strings support `pattern` and `format` (email, hostname, ipv4, ipv6, uuid) but NOT minLength/maxLength. Numbers/integers support const, default, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf. Arrays do NOT support minItems/maxItems. DeepSeek publishes no property-count or nesting-depth ceiling (unlike OpenAI's 100 properties / 5 levels).

max_tool_description_len.notes: No per-request numeric cap documented for the function `description` field. The limits that bind are the 128-function aggregate cap and the 1M context window the serialized descriptions consume as input tokens.

max_request_size.notes: No per-request byte cap documented. The Rate Limit & Isolation page publishes only concurrency limits and a keep-alive rule (the server closes the connection if inference has not started within 10 minutes). Binding limits are the context window and, when self-hosting, the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache).

max_tool_result_size.notes: No per-request numeric cap on a single tool result. Tool results are ordinary message content billed as input tokens, so the binding limit is the 1M context window shared with the 384K output reservation.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No per-request numeric cap on how many tool calls one assistant turn may emit; the Responses API explicitly ignores `max_tool_calls` and always enables parallel tool calling. The binding limits are the 128 functions offered and the output-token budget the tool-call JSON consumes.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No documented server-side cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. Loop length is set by the agent host/framework; the API-side constraints that bind an agent loop are the concurrency limit and the requirement to echo `reasoning_content` back on every tool-carrying request.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a DeepSeek concept — DeepSeek never sees MCP servers (the `mcp` built-in is ignored), so this is set entirely by the MCP host. Host caps that do bind in practice: Cursor ~40 tools total, Claude Desktop ~100.

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Hosted API (model-API layer): 128 functions per request (aggregate), function names <=64 chars matching a-zA-Z0-9_-, concurrency 500 for deepseek-v4-pro and 2500 for deepseek-v4-flash per account across all keys (HTTP 429 above), `user_id` <=512 chars, and the server closes a connection whose inference has not started within 10 minutes. Agent-loop trap: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` MUST be passed back in full or the API returns 400 — this makes thinking-mode tool loops re-send (and re-pay for) their own chain of thought as input. Self-hosted open weights: no model-layer tool-count cap at all; binding limits are the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache), a matching --tool-call-parser for the chat template, and the host app. vLLM's common 16K default context silently truncates tool calls — raise --max-model-len.

strict_function_schema.notes: CHANGED from false: DeepSeek does ship an OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode, in beta (base_url .../beta, `strict: true` on every function, `additionalProperties: false` on every object). It is not identical to OpenAI's: DeepSeek publishes no 100-property / 5-level-depth ceiling, and its unsupported-keyword list is minLength/maxLength/minItems/maxItems (see tool_schema_limits_notes).

skills_supported.notes: No skills/extension mechanism, no persistent memory, no packaged capability bundles.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System prompts are input tokens and are eligible for the disk KV cache. Agentic caveat that dominates real session cost: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` must be passed back in full (400 otherwise), so a thinking-mode tool loop re-submits its own chain of thought as input on every step. Plain multi-turn chat without tools does NOT concatenate previous CoT.

prompt_caching.notes: Disk-based KV cache (context caching), on by default, best-effort. Each request produces cache prefix units at the end of the user input and of the model output, plus units carved at fixed token intervals for long content; entries are cleared when unused, "usually within a few hours to a few days". Usage reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens`. DeepSeek publishes no minimum cacheable prefix size and no explicit statement that tool definitions are separately cacheable — they are cached only as part of a matching prefix. Cache-hit input for deepseek-v4-pro is $0.044/1M peak and $0.022/1M off-peak, against cache-miss input of $1.32/1M peak and $0.66/1M off-peak (peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC; every other hour is off-peak at half rate).

memory_feature.notes: No persistent memory feature in the API.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Cache-MISS input, PEAK rate ($1.32/1M). Off-peak cache-miss input is $0.66/1M. batch_discount.notes: No batch API and no batch discount is published on the Models & Pricing page (re-read 2026-08-19). The only non-list rate is the clock-based off-peak tier — exactly half the peak rate, applying to every hour outside 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC. That is a time-of-day rate, not a batch mode: you cannot opt into it for a latency trade, you can only schedule work into the off-peak hours.

billing_unit.notes: Hosted API bills per token with separate cache-hit / cache-miss input meters. Self-hosting the same open weights carries compute cost only.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: `reasoning_content` is billed at the output rate ($3.96/1M peak, $1.98/1M off-peak; peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC, all other hours off-peak at half) and counts against the 384K output cap. Raising `reasoning_effort` from low to max raises cost on the expensive side of the meter, in both tiers.

weights_url.notes: GA checkpoint. The April preview weights remain published separately at https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

param_variants.value: 1.7T params total (MoE); FP4 experts + FP8 elsewhere
param_variants.notes: CHANGED from "1.6T total / 49B active": the value now agrees with the model's OWN primary card. The DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 repo header states "1.7T params" (tensor types BF16 / I64 / F32 / F8_E4M3 / I8, license mit); the card prose states no total or activated count. Architecture from the same repo's config.json: 61 hidden layers, hidden_size 7168, 384 routed experts, 6 experts per token, 1 shared expert, moe_intermediate_size 3072, 128 attention heads / 1 KV head, quantization_config fp8 (fmt e4m3, weight_block_size [128,128]) with expert_dtype fp4, num_nextn_predict_layers 1, plus a DSpark config block. CONFLICT (kept, not resolved by us): the sibling DeepSeek-V4-Pro-DSpark card states "DeepSeek-V4-Pro with 1.6T parameters (49B activated)" and describes itself as "not a new model ... the same checkpoint with an additional speculative decoding module attached" (its own repo header also reads 1.7T params); the 2026-04-24 V4 preview announcement likewise states "DeepSeek-V4-Pro: 1.6T total / 49B active params". Reading: 1.6T/49B is the transformer architecture figure and 1.7T is the shipped checkpoint total (it includes the bundled next-token-prediction / DSpark module and embeddings). No card states an activated count for the 0813 checkpoint itself, so for MoE serving math use the sibling/announcement figure of ~49B activated per token. Confidence medium because the two tier-1 DeepSeek surfaces disagree.

max_context_documented.notes: Models & Pricing lists CONTEXT LENGTH 1M for deepseek-v4-pro; config.json agrees.

serving_frameworks.notes: The GA card ships launch commands for both. DSpark speculative decoding needs no separate draft model — vLLM: --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}' (with --kv-cache-dtype fp8, --enable-expert-parallel); SGLang: --speculative-algorithm DSPARK.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: Behind vLLM/SGLang's OpenAI-compatible server, tool calling works with the openai_function shape and a matching --tool-call-parser; none of the hosted-API caps (128 functions, 64-char names) are enforced by the weights themselves. MCP still needs a host/adapter that flattens MCP tools into function definitions. In thinking mode with tools, reasoning_content must be carried forward between turns exactly as on the hosted API.

models.notes: GA release 2026-08-13 (news260813), replacing the April 2026 preview checkpoint behind the unchanged `deepseek-v4-pro` model id. function_calling.notes: OpenAI-compatible function calling on /chat/completions, plus function tools on the native Responses API and Anthropic-format tool blocks on the /anthropic endpoint. Tool use works in both thinking and non-thinking modes.

native_mcp.notes: Not MCP-native. The Responses API compatibility table marks the `mcp` built-in tool "Ignored"; the Anthropic-compatible endpoint marks `mcp_servers` "Ignored" and `mcp_tool_use`/`mcp_tool_result` "Not Supported". An MCP host must flatten MCP tools into `function` definitions before sending them.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Upgraded to explicit documentation: on the Responses API "parallel tool calling is always enabled" and `max_tool_calls` is ignored; on the Anthropic-compatible endpoint `disable_parallel_tool_use` is ignored. The model can emit several tool_calls in one assistant turn.

max_tools_hard.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. The cited Chat Completions reference enumerates only hosted aliases for its `model` parameter -- verbatim "Possible values: [`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`]" -- and `deepseek-v4-flash` currently resolves to deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, so the cap does bind anyone calling the hosted endpoint for this checkpoint, and does NOT bind a self-hosted deployment of these weights, where the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang `--tool-call-parser`, `--max-model-len`, KV cache) and the context window consumed by serialized tool definitions set the limits, and an OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of the weights imposes whatever it validates. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the reference states "A max of 128 functions are supported." SCOPE: AGGREGATE -- it counts every function in the request's `tools` array, i.e. all connected MCP servers plus any built-in/host tools combined, not per MCP server. For self-hosted DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 the binding limits are instead the operator's served context length divided by average tool-definition tokens, the empirical selection cliff (see max_tools_practical) and whatever aggregate cap the MCP host imposes (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

max_tools_practical.notes: EMPIRICAL, NOT SPEC, and FAMILY-LEVEL, NOT PER-CHECKPOINT (attribution restated 2026-08-19; tier 4, low confidence). What the cited source actually contains: a single undifferentiated leaderboard entry labelled "DeepSeek V4" reporting 89% single-tool accuracy, 81% at 5 tools and 57% at 20+ tools, with the advice to cap practical tool counts at 15-20 and route/tier above that. It does NOT separate DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek-V4-Flash, does not name a checkpoint (-0813 / -0731), and does not state the serving stack, context length or harness used. The same family-level number is therefore recorded identically on both live checkpoints rather than being split into invented per-variant figures (the same correction convention applied to Gemma's variants and Phi's variants in this dataset). Flash is the smaller, cheaper sibling, so a family figure that blends it with Pro is if anything OPTIMISTIC here -- treat 20 as an upper bound for Flash, not a measured value. The alternative considered was nulling this entry as the weaker attribution of the two; the family figure is kept because the source's leaderboard entry covers the whole V4 generation rather than Pro alone. Scope: AGGREGATE across all connected MCP servers plus built-in tools. Sits far below the hosted API's 128-function cap, and for a self-hosted deployment it is the accuracy cliff -- not any vendor rule -- that binds first.

tool_definition_shape.notes: {type: 'function', function: {name, description, parameters}} on /chat/completions and on the Responses API. The /anthropic endpoint additionally accepts Anthropic tool blocks (name / description / input_schema fully supported). Shape matters for footprint: the same MCP tool serializes to different token counts in the two shapes.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: The serialized `tools` array is part of the prompt and lands in `prompt_tokens`; DeepSeek reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` against that same prompt, so a stable tool-definition prefix is the prime KV-cache candidate. DeepSeek does not state this in one sentence — it follows from the OpenAI-compatible usage object plus the cache guide.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No progressive/deferred tool loading and no server-side tool search. The Responses API supports only function tools, a server-side `web_search`, and the Codex `apply_patch` custom tool; every other built-in (including `mcp`) is ignored. All tool definitions must be resent each request.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Strict mode is a beta feature: call base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/beta", set "strict": true on EVERY function, and set "additionalProperties": false on every object. Supported strict-mode JSON Schema types: object, string, number, integer, boolean, array, enum, anyOf. Strings support `pattern` and `format` (email, hostname, ipv4, ipv6, uuid) but NOT minLength/maxLength. Numbers/integers support const, default, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf. Arrays do NOT support minItems/maxItems. DeepSeek publishes no property-count or nesting-depth ceiling (unlike OpenAI's 100 properties / 5 levels).

max_tool_description_len.notes: No per-request numeric cap documented for the function `description` field. The limits that bind are the 128-function aggregate cap and the 1M context window the serialized descriptions consume as input tokens.

max_request_size.notes: No per-request byte cap documented. The Rate Limit & Isolation page publishes only concurrency limits and a keep-alive rule (the server closes the connection if inference has not started within 10 minutes). Binding limits are the context window and, when self-hosting, the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache).

max_tool_result_size.notes: No per-request numeric cap on a single tool result. Tool results are ordinary message content billed as input tokens, so the binding limit is the 1M context window shared with the 384K output reservation.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No per-request numeric cap on how many tool calls one assistant turn may emit; the Responses API explicitly ignores `max_tool_calls` and always enables parallel tool calling. The binding limits are the 128 functions offered and the output-token budget the tool-call JSON consumes.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No documented server-side cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. Loop length is set by the agent host/framework; the API-side constraints that bind an agent loop are the concurrency limit and the requirement to echo `reasoning_content` back on every tool-carrying request.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a DeepSeek concept — DeepSeek never sees MCP servers (the `mcp` built-in is ignored), so this is set entirely by the MCP host. Host caps that do bind in practice: Cursor ~40 tools total, Claude Desktop ~100.

Self-hosted open weights: no model-layer tool-count cap at all; binding limits are the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache), a matching --tool-call-parser for the chat template, and the host app. vLLM's common 16K default context silently truncates tool calls — raise --max-model-len.

strict_function_schema.notes: CHANGED from false: DeepSeek does ship an OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode, in beta (base_url .../beta, `strict: true` on every function, `additionalProperties: false` on every object). It is not identical to OpenAI's: DeepSeek publishes no 100-property / 5-level-depth ceiling, and its unsupported-keyword list is minLength/maxLength/minItems/maxItems (see tool_schema_limits_notes).

skills_supported.notes: No skills/extension mechanism, no persistent memory, no packaged capability bundles.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System prompts are input tokens and are eligible for the disk KV cache. Agentic caveat that dominates real session cost: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` must be passed back in full (400 otherwise), so a thinking-mode tool loop re-submits its own chain of thought as input on every step. Plain multi-turn chat without tools does NOT concatenate previous CoT.

prompt_caching.notes: Disk-based KV cache (context caching), on by default, best-effort. Each request produces cache prefix units at the end of the user input and of the model output, plus units carved at fixed token intervals for long content; entries are cleared when unused, "usually within a few hours to a few days". Usage reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens`. DeepSeek publishes no minimum cacheable prefix size and no explicit statement that tool definitions are separately cacheable — they are cached only as part of a matching prefix. Cache-hit input for deepseek-v4-flash is $0.014/1M peak and $0.007/1M off-peak, against cache-miss input of $0.44/1M peak and $0.22/1M off-peak (peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC; every other hour is off-peak at half rate).

memory_feature.notes: No persistent memory feature in the API.

batch_discount.notes: No batch API and no batch discount is published on the Models & Pricing page (re-read 2026-08-19). That is a time-of-day rate, not a batch mode: you cannot opt into it for a latency trade, you can only schedule work into the off-peak hours.

billing_unit.notes: Hosted API bills per token with separate cache-hit / cache-miss input meters. Self-hosting the same open weights carries compute cost only.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: `reasoning_content` is billed at the output rate ($1.32/1M peak, $0.66/1M off-peak; peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC, all other hours off-peak at half) and counts against the 384K output cap. Raising `reasoning_effort` from low to max raises cost on the expensive side of the meter, in both tiers.

param_variants.value: 304B params total (MoE); FP4 experts + FP8 elsewhere
param_variants.notes: CHANGED from "284B total / 13B active" (which was cited to the SIBLING DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark card): the value now agrees with the model's OWN primary card. The DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 repo header states "304B params" (tensor types BF16 / I64 / F32 / F8_E4M3 / I8, license MIT); the card prose states no total or activated count, only that the model "outperforms DeepSeek-V4-Pro (Preview) on benchmarks listed below despite its far smaller activated parameter count". Architecture from the same repo's config.json: 43 hidden layers, hidden_size 4096, 256 routed experts, 6 experts per token, 1 shared expert, moe_intermediate_size 2048, quantization_config fp8 (fmt e4m3, weight_block_size [128,128]) with expert_dtype fp4, num_nextn_predict_layers 1, sliding_window 128. CONFLICT (kept, not resolved by us): the sibling DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark card states "DeepSeek-V4-Flash with 284B parameters (13B activated)" and calls itself "not a new model ... the same checkpoint with an additional speculative decoding module attached" (its own repo header reads 165B params — a quantized-checkpoint figure); the 2026-04-24 V4 preview announcement states "DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 284B total / 13B active params", and the 2026-07-31 changelog says "DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 keeps the same model architecture and size as DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Preview, and was only re-post-trained". Reading: 284B/13B is the transformer architecture figure and 304B is the shipped checkpoint total (embeddings plus the bundled next-token-prediction / DSpark module). No card states an activated count for the 0731 checkpoint itself, so for MoE serving math use ~13B activated per token. Confidence medium because the tier-1 DeepSeek surfaces disagree.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: Same as V4-Pro: OpenAI-compatible tool calling out of the box behind vLLM/SGLang with a matching --tool-call-parser; the hosted 128-function and 64-char-name caps are API-layer rules, not weight-level ones. MCP requires a host/adapter.

models.notes: Official release 2026-07-31, replacing the preview behind the unchanged `deepseek-v4-flash` id: same architecture and size, re-post-trained for agentic work, plus native Responses API support, Codex adaptation, low/high/max reasoning effort and a bundled DSpark module. Reported to beat DeepSeek-V4-Pro (Preview) across the published agentic suite (Terminal Bench 2.1 82.7, NL2Repo 54.2, DeepSWE 54.4, Agent Last Exam 25.2) at a fraction of the activated parameters. Cheapest way to run a 1M-context, 128-function tool surface on a first-party endpoint. Legacy aliases `deepseek-chat` / `deepseek-reasoner`, which used to route here, were fully retired after 2026-07-24 15:59 UTC.

The Rate Limit & Isolation page publishes only concurrency limits and a keep-alive rule (the server closes the connection if inference has not started within 10 minutes). Binding limits are the context window and, when self-hosting, the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache).

max_tool_result_size.notes: No per-request numeric cap on a single tool result. Tool results are ordinary message content billed as input tokens, so the binding limit is the 1M context window shared with the 384K output reservation.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No per-request numeric cap on how many tool calls one assistant turn may emit; the Responses API explicitly ignores `max_tool_calls` and always enables parallel tool calling. The binding limits are the 128 functions offered and the output-token budget the tool-call JSON consumes.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No documented server-side cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. Loop length is set by the agent host/framework; the API-side constraints that bind an agent loop are the concurrency limit and the requirement to echo `reasoning_content` back on every tool-carrying request.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a DeepSeek concept — DeepSeek never sees MCP servers (the `mcp` built-in is ignored), so this is set entirely by the MCP host. Host caps that do bind in practice: Cursor ~40 tools total, Claude Desktop ~100.

max_total_tools.notes: No vendor-published per-request numeric cap for self-hosted weights. Effective aggregate ceiling across all connected MCP servers is approximately (context_window - output headroom) / average tool-definition tokens, set by the operator's serving config. Host layers cap lower (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Hosted API (model-API layer): 128 functions per request (aggregate), function names <=64 chars matching a-zA-Z0-9_-, concurrency 500 for deepseek-v4-pro and 2500 for deepseek-v4-flash per account across all keys (HTTP 429 above), `user_id` <=512 chars, and the server closes a connection whose inference has not started within 10 minutes. Agent-loop trap: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` MUST be passed back in full or the API returns 400 — this makes thinking-mode tool loops re-send (and re-pay for) their own chain of thought as input. Self-hosted open weights: no model-layer tool-count cap at all; binding limits are the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache), a matching --tool-call-parser for the chat template, and the host app. vLLM's common 16K default context silently truncates tool calls — raise --max-model-len.

strict_function_schema.notes: Strict function-schema mode is a hosted-API beta feature (base_url .../beta) and V3.2 is no longer served there, so no strict-mode guarantee attaches to these weights; whether a self-hosted server enforces a schema grammar depends on the serving stack.

skills_supported.notes: No skills/extension mechanism, no persistent memory, no packaged capability bundles.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System prompts are input tokens. V3.2 introduced a `developer` role for search-agent scenarios that the official API never accepted. In thinking mode with tools, reasoning_content must be carried forward between turns, so agent loops re-submit their own chain of thought as input.

prompt_caching.notes: DeepSeek's disk KV cache is hosted-API-only and V3.2 is not served there; self-hosted prefix caching depends on the serving framework (vLLM/SGLang automatic prefix caching).

memory_feature.notes: No persistent memory feature in the API.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: OpenAI-compatible tool calling supported in both thinking and non-thinking modes (first DeepSeek model with thinking-in-tool-use). V3.2-Speciale variant does NOT support tool calls. When using thinking mode with tools, reasoning_content must be passed back in subsequent API turns.

models.notes: Released 2025-12-01; now a legacy self-host-only generation. Status changed ga -> deprecated on 2026-08-19: it has no first-party hosted endpoint (Models & Pricing lists only deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-pro), so none of DeepSeek's current hosted-API tool limits (128 functions, 64-char names, beta strict mode, disk KV cache pricing) attach to it. Weights remain published under MIT and it is still the smallest-footprint DeepSeek frontier checkpoint before V4-Flash. Notable for MCP work: first DeepSeek model with reasoning integrated into tool use; 160K context (vs V4's 1M) makes tool-definition footprint ~6.4x more expensive as a share of the window; the Speciale variant cannot call tools at all.
